examples.solution_text:
Graph P starts its vertical scale at $80$. Its bars show only the amounts above $80$, making Library B's bar twice as tall as Library A's.

Library B recorded only $88-84=4$ more loans, so it did not record twice as many.

Graph Q starts at $0$, uses equal scale steps and equal bar widths, and shows both libraries. Its similar bar heights fairly represent the similar totals.

The vertical axis starts at $40$, so cutting off the lower part exaggerates the difference in bar heights.

Venue B's bar is also three times as wide as Venue A's. Its greater area makes the sales difference look much larger than $60-56=4$ tickets.

Use a vertical scale starting at $0$ and equal bar widths.

The number of visitors doubled, but the symbol's area became $2\times2=4$ times as large. This makes a doubling look like a fourfold increase.

If symbol area represents the number of visitors, the second square should have twice the area of the first.

The one-year gap from $2018$ to $2019$ and the four-year gap from $2019$ to $2023$ are drawn equally wide.

Membership increased by $20$ in each interval, but the second increase took four years. Equal spacing hides the slower increase after $2019$.

Space the years according to the actual time gaps.

The reported shares total $50\%+45\%+35\%=130\%$.

Each student selected exactly one activity, and all choices are included, so these shares must total $100\%$. The graph cannot be a correct breakdown of this survey.

No. The vertical axis has no numerical scale, so the sales totals and their difference cannot be read.

March's bar is taller, showing more sales, but the graph does not tell us how many more. Add a labelled vertical scale.

examples.derivation: Graph P represents 84 and 88 as heights (84−80)/2=2 and (88−80)/2=4, creating a twofold height comparison. The actual difference is 88−84=4 loans. Graph Q represents the same totals as 84/20=4.2 and 88/20=4.4, with a zero baseline, equal steps and equal widths. This matches Book 3 Foundation 1 and Mastery 12. Separate graph blocks and increased axis-title offsets address the diagnosed collisions in the authored structure.

The plotted heights are (56−40)/5=3.2 and (60−40)/5=4. The widths are 0.6 and 1.8, so B is three times as wide. Both the truncated baseline and unequal widths exaggerate an actual difference of 4 tickets. Identifying these two features follows Book 3 Mastery 13.

The visitor ratio is 300/150=2. The square areas are 1×1=1 and 2×2=4 coordinate units, producing an area ratio of 4. The diagram therefore exaggerates the doubling. This adapts the changing-width-and-height distortion in Book 3 Mastery 15 without introducing square-root sizing.

The points represent 20, 40 and 60 members. Both horizontal gaps are 2 coordinate units, although the elapsed times are 1 year and 4 years. Equal increases of 20 took different durations, so equal plotted slopes conceal the slower later increase. This follows Book 3 Foundation 4f and Mastery 15.

The bar heights encode 2.5×20%=50%, 2.25×20%=45% and 1.75×20%=35%, agreeing with their annotations. Their sum is 130%. Exactly one selection per student across all included categories requires a total of 100%, so the reported breakdown is impossible. This adapts Book 3 Mastery 10 within the target skill. Moving the vertical title to x=−2 separates it from the percentage ticks in the authored structure.

January and March have plotted heights 1.5 and 3, but no numerical vertical scale converts those heights into item counts. The graph communicates an ordering but cannot supply the numerical difference. This follows the missing-scale feature in Book 3 Foundation 4c.
